target.title: VSpeechLM: A Visual Speech Language Model for Visual Text-to-Speech Task

read.pdf: Figures 1–4, Tables 1–4 read as represented in text.txt; no separate PDF available

entries.text: VSpeechLM uses a phoneme–lip text-video aligner to produce an expanded phoneme sequence, then SpeechLLM decoders generate speech.
entries.condition: Input text, video, reference speech; aligner-trained expanded phonemes used at inference.
entries.quote: we propose a text-video aligner

entries.text: Authors claim state-of-the-art performance on two datasets over multiple speech quality, similarity, intelligibility, and synchronization metrics.
entries.condition: Chem and GRID; evaluated metrics in Table 1.

entries.text: AV-HuBERT lip embeddings are sampled from video frames at 25 fps and have dimension 1024.
entries.condition: Video modality representation.

entries.text: EnCodec represents speech with 8 hierarchical codebooks at 16 kHz.
entries.condition: Both reference and target speech are discretized.
entries.quote: The sample rate is 16k Hz.

entries.text: Aligner supervision uses Montreal Forced Aligner phoneme durations to form the ground-truth expanded phoneme sequence; aligner and decoder are jointly optimized.
entries.condition: Training decoder sees ground-truth expanded phonemes; inference uses predicted expanded phonemes.
entries.quote: During the training stage, we use the ground truth expanded phoneme sequence

entries.text: Decoder is initialized from pretrained ESPnet models; AdamW initial LR 1e-4, betas (0.9, 0.95); top-k 30, temperature 1.2 Chem and 0.5 GRID.
entries.condition: Inference settings vary by dataset; remaining architecture/training detail deferred to supplement.

entries.text: Chem has 6,240 train, 200 validation, 200 test samples; GRID has 33 speakers and 1,000 clips each, with 32,670 train and 900 test samples.
entries.condition: English datasets; Chem single-speaker; GRID multi-speaker; 100 clips per speaker selected for GRID test.

entries.text: Chem test: VSpeechLM WER 12.5, speaker similarity 78.9, UTMOS 3.73, MCD-DTW 5.16, MCD-DTW-SL 5.28.
entries.unit: WER%; Spk Sim; UTMOS; MCD-DTW; MCD-DTW-SL
entries.condition: Chem test set; Table 1; inference uses top-k 30, temperature 1.2; scores compared to reported baseline WER/MCD and generated-checkpoint UTMOS/Spk Sim.

entries.text: GRID test: VSpeechLM WER 18.3, speaker similarity 69.7, UTMOS 3.94, MCD-DTW 3.91, MCD-DTW-SL 3.90.
entries.unit: WER%; Spk Sim; UTMOS; MCD-DTW; MCD-DTW-SL
entries.condition: GRID test set, 900 clips from 33 speakers; top-k 30, temperature 0.5; Table 1 evaluation protocol.

entries.text: Chem EmoDubber comparison scores: WER 12.8, Spk Sim 78.1, UTMOS 3.87, MCD-DTW 6.51, MCD-DTW-SL 6.51.
entries.unit: WER%; Spk Sim; UTMOS; MCD-DTW; MCD-DTW-SL
entries.condition: Chem; baselines' WER/MCD scores reported from prior paper; UTMOS/Spk Sim generated with public checkpoint.

entries.text: GRID StyleDubber comparison scores: WER 19.6, Spk Sim 67.0, UTMOS 3.73, MCD-DTW 6.33, MCD-DTW-SL 6.42.
entries.unit: WER%; Spk Sim; UTMOS; MCD-DTW; MCD-DTW-SL
entries.condition: GRID; objective comparison; protocols as Table 1 caption.

entries.text: Authors report MCD-DTW-SL reductions of 17.6% versus EmoDubber on Chem and 60.9% versus StyleDubber on GRID.
entries.condition: Chem/EmoDubber and GRID/StyleDubber respectively; duration consistency metric.
entries.quote: there are improvements of 17.6% (vs. EmoDubber) and 60.9% (vs. StyleDubber) reduction respectively

entries.text: UTMOS is second-best, 0.04 below the codec decoder upper bound; authors suggest codec quality may constrain further gains and plan to explore alternatives.
entries.condition: Objective evaluation; codec decoder upper bound.

entries.text: Human evaluation compares against EmoDubber on Chem and StyleDubber on GRID using 50 test clips per dataset and 10 expert raters; four criteria, winner/tie choice.
entries.condition: Criteria: speech quality, lip synchronization, speaker similarity, expressiveness.
entries.quote: We sampled 50 clips each from the test sets of Chem and GRID.

entries.text: Authors say their system wins over the selected strongest baselines across all four subjective criteria; GRID has many ties in expressiveness and synchronization.
entries.condition: Subjective comparison: Chem vs EmoDubber, GRID vs StyleDubber.

entries.text: Chem ablation: aligner WER 12.48, Spk Sim 78.87, UTMOS 3.73, MCD-DTW-SL 5.28; no visual 15.02/76.91/3.81/6.49; visual prefix 15.16/74.38/3.51/6.94.
entries.unit: WER%; Spk Sim; UTMOS; MCD-DTW-SL, per configuration
entries.condition: Chem dataset; three visual-input configurations; Table 2.
entries.quote: Ablating visual integration methods on the Chem dataset.

entries.text: Chem training ablation: full model 12.5/78.9/3.87/5.28; no pretraining 151/50.6/1.62/13.99; no adapting 829/2.86/1.49/80.92.
entries.unit: WER%; Spk Sim; UTMOS; MCD-DTW-SL, per configuration
entries.condition: Chem; no pretraining means random decoder; no adapting means pretrained decoder frozen and only aligner adapted.

entries.text: Zero-shot LRS2 scores: VSpeechLM WER 16.1, Spk Sim 53.9, UTMOS 2.98, MCD-DTW-SL 7.59; evaluated systems include GT, HPMDubbing, StyleDubber, EmoDubber.
entries.condition: 200 randomly sampled LRS2 clips; zero-shot; noisy audio and non-frontal faces; no training adaptation stated.

entries.text: Authors claim the model has the best performance on LRS2 and robustness in challenging real-world conditions.
entries.condition: Zero-shot 200 randomly sampled LRS2 clips; Table 4 metrics.

entries.text: Authors identify partially invisible lip motion and low-quality video as challenging scenarios for future work.
entries.condition: Deployment robustness limitations acknowledged in conclusion.

entries.text: The paper does not report random seeds, repeated runs, confidence intervals, or statistical significance for objective or subjective results.
entries.condition: All reported evaluations.

entries.text: Test speaker overlap and speaker-disjointness between GRID train and test are not specified; GRID test clips are sampled per speaker.
entries.condition: GRID 33 speakers, 100 test clips per speaker; paper does not state held-out speakers.

entries.text: Selection/validation data used for checkpoint selection, hyperparameter tuning, or early stopping are not described.
entries.condition: Chem validation set stated but its use is not stated; GRID validation set not reported.

entries.text: Text does not specify metric normalization, ASR/embedding model versions, scorer details, or full MCD-DTW/MCD-DTW-SL computation; details are deferred to supplementary material.
entries.condition: Objective metrics; GRID WER is acknowledged to be imperfect even for ground truth.

entries.text: No chance level or uncertainty around expert win/tie/loss judgments is provided in the accessible paper text.
entries.condition: Human preference evaluation shown graphically in Figure 3.
entries.quote: The scoring was done by selecting a winner or declaring a tie for each comparison.

entries.text: LRS2 clip sampling procedure beyond random sampling and sample count, along with speaker composition and scoring protocol, is not specified.
entries.condition: Zero-shot LRS2 evaluation.

entries.text: Table 1 mixes baseline provenance: WER/MCD values follow baseline reported results while UTMOS and speaker similarity are reproduced from public checkpoints.
entries.condition: Comparability differs across metric families.
entries.quote: For UTMOS and Spk Sim, we use their public checkpoint to generate speech and evaluate.

entries.text: Table 1 GT row: Chem WER 3.87, Spk Sim 100, UTMOS 4.19; GRID WER 22.5, Spk Sim 100, UTMOS 4.04.
entries.condition: Ground-truth recordings scored with the paper's ASR.

entries.text: Table 1 GT (decoder) row (codec resynthesis upper bound): Chem WER 3.89, Spk Sim 99.8, UTMOS 3.77, MCD-DTW 2.60, MCD-DTW-SL 2.61; GRID WER 22.6, Spk Sim 93.3, UTMOS 3.98, MCD-DTW 2.62, MCD-DTW-SL 2.66.
Table 1 HPMDubbing row: Chem WER 29.8, Spk Sim 44.6, UTMOS 3.11, MCD-DTW 6.91, MCD-DTW-SL 8.56; GRID WER 44.2, Spk Sim 31.3, UTMOS 2.11, MCD-DTW 6.79, MCD-DTW-SL 7.09.
Table 1 StyleDubber row: Chem WER 14.2, Spk Sim 73.7, UTMOS 3.14, MCD-DTW 6.01, MCD-DTW-SL 6.36; GRID WER 19.6, Spk Sim 67.0, UTMOS 3.73, MCD-DTW 6.33, MCD-DTW-SL 6.42.
Table 1 EmoDubber row: Chem WER 12.8, Spk Sim 78.1, UTMOS 3.87, MCD-DTW 6.51, MCD-DTW-SL 6.51; GRID WER 19.8, Spk Sim 50.5, UTMOS 3.98, MCD-DTW 3.92, MCD-DTW-SL 3.92.
Synchronization is assessed only by MCD-DTW-SL (duration synchronization); no LSE-C, LSE-D or SyncNet score appears in the paper.
entries.quote:
and MCD-DTW weighted by speech length
(MCD-DTW-SL)[3] to assess duration synchronization.

entries.text: Authors: VSpeechLM is second best on UTMOS, behind EmoDubber, and 0.04 from the codec decoder upper bound (GT (decoder) row).
The text does not explain why Chem UTMOS is 3.87 for Table 3 (a) Ours but 3.73 in Tables 1 and 2.
entries.quote:
‘w/o pretraining’ indicates that the decoder is randomly
initialized and trained only with VisualTTS.

entries.text: Decoders initialised from ESPnet pretrained models and all modules trained jointly; pretraining corpus and hours not stated.
entries.quote:
We initialize VSpeechLM decoders from
ESPnet [27, 28] pretrained models and jointly train all modules.

entries.text: The aligner classifies each lip frame to a phoneme (cross-entropy on MFA-derived labels); at inference each frame takes the most similar phoneme; no duration predictor or monotonic constraint is described.
entries.quote:
where each lip movement corresponds to a ground-truth phoneme
in the dataset.

entries.text: Authors: DubWise feeds video into a SpeechLLM via cross-attention but controls only global duration.
entries.quote:
DubWise [24] attempts to incorporate video features into Speech-
LLM via cross-attention, but only control global duration without
fine temporal alignment.

entries.text: Table 4 LRS2 zero-shot rows: GT 8.52/1.00/3.14/0.00; HPMDubbing 198/33.2/1.28/8.43; StyleDubber 91.4/50.3/1.87/14.0; EmoDubber 110/10.3/1.70/8.68; VSpeechLM 16.1/53.9/2.98/7.59 (WER, Spk Sim, UTMOS, MCD-DTW-SL).
Table 4 does not say whether the baselines were also applied zero-shot or on which data they were trained.
entries.quote:
Table 4: Zero-shot evaluation results of VSpeechLM on 200
randomly sampled clips from the LRS2 dataset.

entries.text: No inference speed, real-time factor, parameter count or compute is reported.
The ASR model for WER and the speaker model for Spk Sim are not named.
Human evaluation gives no win/tie/loss percentages in the text (Fig. 3 only).

entries.text: DiFlowDubber GRID Table 2, Setting 1.0: LSE-C 7.32, LSE-D 6.73, WER 16.79, SECS 82.52, UTMOS 3.95; EmoDubber 7.12, 6.82, 18.53, 92.22, 3.83. Setting 2.0: EmoDubber WER 19.75, DiFlowDubber 16.21.
entries.condition: GRID test; Whisper-V3; Setting 1.0

entries.text: WER is computed with Whisper-V3; SECS is speaker-encoder cosine similarity.
entries.quote:
Whisper-V3 [45] as
the automatic speech recognition system. Additionally, we
use Speaker Encoder Cosine Similarity (SECS)

entries.text: The Synchronizer aligns video with text and speech with text (dual alignment); per the reader, cross-attention plus monotonic alignment search gives phoneme-to-frame durations.
entries.quote:
It enhances video-
speech alignment through the dual-alignment mechanism:
video-text alignment, and speech-text alignment, which to-
gether enforce robust cross-modal synchronization.

entries.text: MOS-S: 20 listeners rate 30 randomly selected samples on a 1-5 scale for similarity to the reference.
Compared baselines are earlier dubbing systems (V2C-Net, HPMDubbing, StyleDubber, Speaker2Dubber, ProDubber, EmoDubber); VSpeechLM is not compared.

Visual TTS: visual embeddings attend over phoneme embeddings of lip-read (VTP) text, the result is upsampled and decoded to mel-spectrograms, so the video-text alignment sets phoneme duration without a separate duration predictor.
entries.quote:
using this attention
mechanism. After adding the speaker identity embedding, these are then upsampled and decoded into melspectrograms.

entries.text: Mel-spectrograms are converted to waveform by the pretrained BigVGAN vocoder.
LRS2 test: with VTP lip-read text (L2T-WER 22.6) LSE-C 8.083, LSE-D 6.586; with ground-truth text LSE-C 8.781, LSE-D 6.106.
Hegde et al., Towards Accurate Lip-to-Speech Synthesis in-the-Wild, ACM MM 2023.
LipAdapter derives hard phoneme durations from lip-phoneme soft alignment with monotonic alignment search and feeds the length-regulated phonemes to a pretrained TTS (ZMM-TTS).
entries.quote:
Monotonic Alignment Search is applied to soft alignment to derive hard phoneme
durations aligned with video frames.

entries.text: At inference the text is predicted by a pretrained VSR model (V+T input).
LRS3: LipAdapter WER 21.2%, LSE-C 6.165, LSE-D 8.250 with 30 h of training video; LipVoicer 21.4%, 5.803, 8.637 with 430 h.
LipAdapter title and authors (Ghosh, Jawahar, Namboodiri; Interspeech 2026).
GRID: 33 speakers with 1,000 clips each; 100 clips per speaker selected for testing, stated to give 32,670 training and 900 test samples.
entries.unit: speakers; clips; clips per speaker; samples
entries.quote: with 33 speakers and 1,000 clips of each speaker. Following [8, 9], we select 100 clips per speaker for testing, resulting in 32,670 training and 900 test samples.

entries.text: Which utterance serves as reference speech at test time (the target utterance itself or another utterance of the speaker) is not stated; the reference is described only as part of the decoder prompt.
entries.quote: The reference speech serves as part of the prompt input to VSpeechLM’s decoder, providing speaker identity information.

entries.text: Human evaluation compares against EmoDubber on Chem and StyleDubber on GRID.
entries.quote: we compared our method with EmoDubber on the Chem dataset and with StyleDubber on the GRID dataset.

entries.text: Authors attribute the Spk Sim lead to in-context learning without an external speaker encoder.
Authors: previous VisualTTS models are primarily based on FastSpeech2 or flow-matching TTS backbones.
entries.quote: Previous VisualTTS models [ 7–9, 16, 31] are primarily based on lightweight TTS backbones such as FastSpeech2 [22] or flow-matching TTS models [19].

entries.text: Authors: GRID WER is suboptimal even for ground-truth audio because the ASR misrecognizes liaison and non-standard pronunciation.
entries.quote: leading to suboptimal WER even for ground-truth audio.

entries.text: Fig. 3 shows win-tie-loss ratios; the authors note many ties on GRID for expressiveness and synchronization.
entries.quote: (a) shows win-tie-loss ratios against EmoDubber on Chem, and (b) against StyleDubber on GRID.

entries.text: Training feeds the decoder the ground-truth expanded phoneme sequence; inference uses the predicted one.
entries.quote: During the training stage, we use the ground truth expanded phoneme sequence

entries.text: DiFlowDubber Chem table, Setting 2.0 (non-ground-truth reference): HPMDubbing WER 29.82, StyleDubber 14.18; Setting 1.0: 16.05, 13.14. Prior systems V2C-Net (CVPR 22), HPMDubbing (CVPR 23), StyleDubber (ACL 24) carry LSE-C/LSE-D values.
